scenes.narration: Drug-resistant bacteria directly caused an estimated 1.27 million deaths worldwide in 2019.
scenes.title: WHY ANTIBIOTICS STOP WORKING

scenes.narration: Counting every death they contributed to, the toll reaches 4.95 million people.
scenes.caption: 4.95 M

scenes.narration: In 1945, Alexander Fleming warned that underdosing would breed resistant microbes. It is plain selection: the drug kills the weak and the resistant multiply.
Plasmids copy resistance genes from one bacterium to another, even across different species.
Biofilms add a slimy shield, making bacteria up to 1,000 times more tolerant.
Meanwhile, nearly all new antibiotics are tweaks of classes found by the 1980s.
scenes.caption: RECYCLED CLASSES
scenes.sub: WHO: almost all new drugs are variants of old classes

scenes.narration: WHO counts only 15 truly innovative drugs among 90 in clinical development.
scenes.caption: 15 OF 90

scenes.narration: The comeback may be phages, which are viruses that hunt bacteria. A Belgian-led review of 100 personalised phage cases found 77 percent improved.
That was not a controlled trial, so the evidence is still fairly thin.
scenes.caption: NOT A TRIAL
scenes.sub: retrospective and uncontrolled · Pirnay et al. 2024

scenes.narration: Resistance is not medicine failing; it is evolution simply doing its job. Follow for more.
